title: What Is Matcha? A Guide to Japanese Green Tea Powder
meta_description: Matcha is finely-ground Japanese green tea, shade-grown and whisked into water. What makes it different from green tea, how it's made, and how to brew it.
body_html:
Matcha is a stone-ground powder made from shade-grown Japanese green tea leaves. Unlike steeped tea, you whisk the entire leaf into water and drink it — meaning every cup delivers the full nutritional profile of the plant.

How matcha is made

Three to four weeks before harvest, tea farmers cover the tea bushes with shade cloth. The lack of sunlight forces the plant to produce more chlorophyll and L-theanine, giving matcha its bright green color and characteristic umami sweetness.

After harvest, leaves are steamed to halt oxidation, dried, de-stemmed, and stone-ground into a powder so fine it floats on water.

Matcha grades

  • Ceremonial grade — first-harvest leaves, brightest color, most delicate flavor. Whisk with water only.
  • Premium grade — second harvest, slightly more astringent. Daily-drinking matcha.
  • Culinary grade — later harvest, stronger flavor, holds up in lattes and baking.

How to brew matcha

  1. Sift 1–2 grams (about ½ tsp) of matcha into a warm bowl.
  2. Add 60ml of water heated to 70°C / 160°F.
  3. Whisk in a rapid W or M motion until a fine foam forms (~15 seconds).
  4. Drink immediately — matcha settles fast.

Matcha vs. regular green tea

Regular green tea is steeped and discarded. Matcha is consumed in full, so the caffeine, L-theanine, and antioxidant content per cup is roughly 3–4× higher. Published research has looked at how L-theanine and caffeine interact in combination — see "What the science measures" below for what that research actually recorded.

Zen tradition

The Zen monk Eisai brought tea seeds to Japan in 1191 and, 23 years later, wrote Kissa Yōjōki ("Drink Tea, Prolong Life," 1214 CE), the first Japanese treatise on tea as medicine. Zen monasteries used matcha to sustain the alert calm needed for long meditation — the same state zazen trains for, brought into the cup.

What the science measures

A 2008 study (Kelly et al., J Nutrition) recorded EEG alpha-band activity (8–14 Hz, the brain rhythm of relaxed attention) in subjects given L-theanine + caffeine versus either alone. The combination produced a distinctive alpha-band signature linked to focused, calm cognition — the same oscillation pattern seen in experienced meditators.

This describes published research and general information, not medical or dietary advice.

Spilling the Beans: How Much Caffeine Is Too Much?

faqs.a: Matcha (1 tsp / 2 g) has less caffeine than coffee — roughly 65–70 mg versus about 95 mg in an 8 oz brewed cup (see our matcha caffeine breakdown). It also carries a meaningfully higher dose of L-theanine, an amino acid concentrated in tea, than most drinks. A 2008 study (Kelly et al., Journal of Nutrition, PMID 18641209) found that L-theanine combined with caffeine was associated with changes in EEG alpha-band brain activity and attention-task performance compared with either alone — a description of what that research measured, not a promise about how any individual cup will feel.

faqs.q: How much matcha can I drink per day?
faqs.a: There's no single number that's right for everyone, but here's what's published: the U.S. FDA has cited about 400 mg of caffeine per day as a general reference point for healthy adults that isn't generally associated with dangerous, negative effects. A standard 2 g (1 tsp) matcha serving has roughly 65–70 mg of caffeine (see our matcha caffeine breakdown), so a couple of servings a day is a modest share of that reference — though it's worth counting all caffeinated drinks together, not matcha alone. People who are pregnant, caffeine-sensitive, or managing a health condition should talk to a healthcare provider about what's appropriate for them.
Matcha doesn't spoil but it does fade. Sealed tins keep peak flavor for about 6 months in a cool, dark place; once opened, finish within 4–6 weeks.
